title: AI log
text: I used an AI assistant (Claude) throughout this project. My prompts were written in Russian; below they are translated and shortened. This is not the whole conversation. It is the set of exchanges that changed the project or my understanding of it, which is what the assignment asks for.

title: AI log
section: Who did what
text:
Who did what







I decided
The AI did




The theme: local food, after testing my own idea of fast food on the data
Wrote the R code, the report text and the site


To keep seafood in the theme, against the AI’s first recommendation
Ran a test on the real data whenever I questioned a choice


To divide the city the way people talk about it, not only the way the data does
Looked up how New Orleans is divided, and found the planning districts


The four scoring rules, after having them explained twice
Checked its own work, and reported the mistakes it found (listed at the end)


To name one best part of town, with the uncertainty stated
Tried 24 ways of scoring areas to see whether one winner was real


What goes public and what stays private
Kept a log of every decision and who made it

title: AI log
section: Iteration 1: “Is the bootstrap required, or is it your idea?”
text:
Iteration 1: “Is the bootstrap required, or is it your idea?”
The AI proposed showing how stable the top ten is with a bootstrap. I liked it, then stopped.
My prompt: “The bootstrap you are proposing: is that something the assignment expects, or is it purely your idea?”
Answer: its idea. It searched the assignment text: the word never appears. The assignment asks to define “best” using “the reliability of the comparison” and names no method.
My next prompt: “Is what you proposed the best there is? Keep in mind the complexity has to be reasonable. This is Math 167R.”
Answer: it backed off to a simpler tool, a plus-or-minus interval around each average, and computed it.
My next prompt: “The level of the class is something to keep in mind, but this is a university statistics project. If there is a better option in that sense, we should probably stick with it.”
Answer: it agreed that I was right and it had over-read my earlier message. An interval says how well one average is known. It does not say how far a rank can move, and star ratings are skewed and capped at five. Final design: intervals for the picture, the bootstrap for the number.
My last prompt in the chain: “Explain in simple words, as if I were ten, what the bootstrap is and how exactly it helps.”
What I took from it: put every review of a restaurant in a hat, draw the same number back out with repeats allowed, recompute the average, rank everyone again, and do that 2,000 times. I accepted the method only once I could explain it this way myself.

title: AI log
section: Iteration 2: “Maybe we should just do fast food?”
text:
Iteration 2: “Maybe we should just do fast food?”
The AI found that Yelp’s “Seafood” label pulls Peruvian and Ethiopian restaurants into a local-food theme. I thought the theme was getting complicated.
My prompt: “If this local-food category is going to be this complicated, maybe we shouldn’t take it and should take something like fast food instead?”
Answer, tested on the data: fast food has the same label problem (its trial top ten held an Italian deli, a grocery store and a gelato cafe), a quarter of its restaurants are chain locations, and the “Fast Food” label alone has 80 active reviewers.
Decision (mine): local food. “It is New Orleans, so that is the food people want to know about.”

title: AI log
section: Iteration 3: “I don’t want to just get rid of seafood”
text:
Iteration 3: “I don’t want to just get rid of seafood”
The AI recommended dropping the Seafood category to keep the theme clean.
My prompt: “Seafood is something a lot of people love, and I don’t want to drop it just because it has problems. Maybe there is a way to handle seafood specially? Think about it, and if you still think it is better without, then fine.”
What happened: the AI read all 106 open restaurants that would enter only through that label. Most were plainly local: Drago’s, GW Fins, Pêche, Parkway Bakery. It said my instinct was better than its recommendation, and wrote a rule: Seafood counts, unless the restaurant got in only through that label and Yelp also gives it another country’s cuisine.
Result: 608 restaurants instead of 508, with the well-known seafood houses in and the sushi bars out.

title: AI log
section: Iteration 4: “How do people usually divide New Orleans?”
text:
Iteration 4: “How do people usually divide New Orleans?”
The AI recommended the 72 official neighborhoods.
My prompt: “I want the way we divide the city to match how other people usually divide it, so it is obvious at once which area we mean. Could you search the web for how this is done in New Orleans? And is my idea a good one or not?”
What it found: the 72 neighborhoods are statistical units, and the organization that publishes them warns that residents picture their neighborhoods differently. The city’s tourism site and its planning commission both use about a dozen larger areas: Uptown, Mid-City, Marigny and Bywater.
Result: two levels. Planning districts for “which part of town”, neighborhoods for the detail inside. With districts, 99% of restaurants sit in an area large enough to compare, against 78% with neighborhoods.

title: AI log
section: Iteration 5: “How do these rules work with the bootstrap?”
text:
Iteration 5: “How do these rules work with the bootstrap?”
The AI proposed ranking restaurants by a reviewer-adjusted score.
My prompts: “Explain the problem again, and why you want exactly these four rules.” Then: “Before I accept them: how will they work with the method we used for the top ten?”
What happened: to answer, the AI ran the bootstrap on top of its own proposal, and the result changed its recommendation. The adjusted score uses only 23% of the reviews, so its top ten is noisy: 7.4 of the ten survive a reshuffle on average, against 8.7 for the plain average.
Result: rank by the plain average, and use the adjusted score as a check. Eight of the ten pass it.

title: AI log
section: Iteration 6: “Is it really a tie? Recheck everything.”
text:
Iteration 6: “Is it really a tie? Recheck everything.”
The first area results showed four parts of town within 0.01 stars of each other.
My prompt: “Did it really come out that several parts are best? Recheck everything. Maybe there is a better way to compute the scores. I would like to name one best part, even if it is a stretch.”
What happened: the AI recomputed everything from the raw reviews (identical numbers), then tried 24 ways of scoring an area. The winner changed with the method, which is what a real tie looks like. It told me that choosing a formula because it produces a winner is exactly what the assignment warns against.
What it offered instead: the question asks where to find the best restaurants, so the right measure is the share of an area’s restaurants in the city’s top quarter. On that measure one district leads, with 10 of 27, and comes first in half of the reshuffles.
My follow-up: “Explain again: what is the 10% threshold about?” With a stricter cut-off another district leads, on a count of 3 restaurants out of 16 against 3 out of 27. I chose 25% once I understood why.

title: AI log
section: Iteration 7: “Was the benchmark in the assignment?”
text:
Iteration 7: “Was the benchmark in the assignment?”
The AI measured three ways of reading the 5 GB file without asking me.
My prompt: “What is this whole benchmark for? Was all of this in the assignment or what?”
Answer: no. The assignment asks for a section on handling large data; the measurement was the AI’s addition, and it said it should have asked first. I kept it as one table: reading the whole file takes 18 GB of memory, reading in chunks takes 2 GB.

title: AI log
section: Iteration 8: the site
text:
Iteration 8: the site
My prompts, in order: “I don’t like any of these” (three homepage sketches). “Let’s brainstorm: what could we make that is actually good?” “When someone scrolls, something should always be happening.” “Better fonts, and make the text sound like a person wrote it.” “I want to rework the art direction. Look at how the last project was made. Don’t copy its style, just look at how professional and minimal it was.”
What changed: the three sketches were one layout in three color schemes, and the AI agreed that was why they felt generic. The concept I chose makes the finding visible without a number: every restaurant is a light, brightness is the number of reviews, color is the rating, flicker is uncertainty.
The first build had glowing halos, film grain, gradients and a blurred glass card. After my last prompt the AI compared it with Project 1 and stripped all of that: one flat background, hairlines, flat dots sized by the number of reviews, and one accent color that only ever marks the best quarter.

title: AI log
section: What the AI got wrong, and how it was caught
text:
What the AI got wrong, and how it was caught

Block group names were not unique. “Block Group 2” exists in every census tract, so 440 areas collapsed into 6. Caught by the AI when a table came out wrong; fixed and guarded with a check.
It recommended dropping Seafood because it was simpler, not because it was better. Caught by me.
It read “keep it at the level of the class” as “use the simplest method”. Caught by me.
It claimed a result held “in 100% of reshuffles” on a measure where that was not true. Caught by the AI when it computed the number, and corrected in the same message.
It added a benchmark without asking. Caught by me.
The site and the report rounded two numbers differently (4.46 against 4.47, 95% against 94%). Caught by the AI when it compared every figure on the site with the report.
The template code it started from had three bugs of its own: review dates parsed with the wrong function, a filter on a column that did not exist yet, and a table that was never created.

title: AI log
section: What I would tell someone doing this
text:
What I would tell someone doing this
Ask “is this required or is it your idea?” early. Ask for the explanation again until you could give it yourself. And when the AI agrees with you quickly, ask it to test the idea on the data first.

title: Where to eat local in New Orleans
text:
TipIn plain words



I used 6,990,280 Yelp reviews to find the best places for local food in New Orleans: Cajun and Creole cooking, Southern food, soul food and seafood. Two things came out. The ten best restaurants are spread over 6 parts of the city, and only 2 of them are in the French Quarter. And the part of town where your chance of walking into a great place is highest is Mid-City / Tremé / Bayou St. John, not the tourist center. A top-ten list from star ratings is never exact, so for every restaurant I also report how likely it is to really belong in the top ten.

title: Where to eat local in New Orleans
section: Executive summary
text:
Executive summary
Question. Where can someone find the best local-food restaurants in New Orleans, and which geographic area is best for finding them?
Data. The Yelp Open Dataset: 6,990,280 reviews in one 4.98 GB file. After filtering to the city and the theme, the analysis uses 238,474 reviews of 608 restaurants written by 134,104 reviewers between March 2005 and January 2022.
Answer.

The top ten. Heard Dat Kitchen, Sweet Soulfood, Restaurant Rebirth lead the list; the full ten are in the first table below. 7 of them are in the top ten in at least 90% of 2,000 resamples of the reviews. The last places are a close race: 18 restaurants have a realistic chance at ten places.
The best part of town. Mid-City / Tremé / Bayou St. John: 10 of its 27 ranked restaurants (37%) are in the best quarter of the city, against 17% in the French Quarter. Its lead over Central City / Garden District (33%) is small: it comes first in 50% of resamples.
Reviewer habits change little. After adjusting each rating for how generous its reviewer usually is, 8 of the ten restaurants are still in the top ten.

title: Where to eat local in New Orleans
section: The answer first
text:
The answer first
A restaurant is ranked by the average of all its star ratings. To be ranked it must be open and have at least 30 reviews from active reviewers (people with five or more reviews of local-food restaurants). 231 restaurants qualify. The reasons for each rule are in the sections below.


Show code
top10 |>
  transmute(
    Rank = rank,
    Restaurant = business_name,
    `Part of town` = part_of_town,
    Reviews = n(reviews_all),
    `Average stars` = f2(ordinary_average),
    Interval = paste(f2(ordinary_low), "to", f2(ordinary_high)),
    `Chance of being top 10` = pct(ordinary_chance_top10),
    `Still top 10 after reviewer adjustment` = ifelse(also_top10_after_adjustment, "yes", paste0("no (rank ", rank_adjusted, ")"))
  ) |>
  kable(align = "rllrrlrl")

title: Where to eat local in New Orleans
section: The data, and how I handled a 5 GB file
text:
The data, and how I handled a 5 GB file
The Yelp Open Dataset comes as one 4.35 GB zip archive. Inside the zip is a tar archive, and inside that are five JSON files with one record per line. I needed two of them.



File
Size
Rows




yelp_academic_dataset_business.json
0.11 GB
150,346


yelp_academic_dataset_review.json
4.98 GB
6,990,280



Problems and what I did about them.

An archive inside an archive, and limited reason to unpack all of it. The two files I needed take 5.5 GB once unpacked. I extracted only those two, left the other three (users, tips and check-ins) packed, and deleted the intermediate tar.
The review file does not fit comfortably in memory. The assignment’s template reads it in one call. I measured that: it works on my computer only because it has 48 GB of memory. R/01_import.R instead reads 100,000 lines at a time and keeps only the rows and columns it needs from each chunk.
Most of the file is not about New Orleans. Only 761,673 of the 6,990,280 reviews (11%) are about a Louisiana business. They are filtered during the import, so the full file is never held at once.
Review text is the heavy part. The analysis uses only the star rating, so the text is dropped. The final review table (238,474 rows) is a 9 MB compressed .rds file.
Raw files cannot go to GitHub. GitHub rejects files over 100 MB. data/raw/ is listed in .gitignore; the repository holds only the filtered tables.
Two bugs in the template code. Review dates are timestamps such as 2018-07-07 22:09:11, so ymd() returns missing values and ymd_hms() is needed. And block group names such as “Block Group 2” repeat in every census tract, so they must be combined with the tract number before they can identify an area.

Three ways to read the file, measured. Each method ran in its own R process and had to read the same 6,990,280 rows and keep the same 761,673.


Show code
benchmark |>
  mutate(Method = c(chunked    = "Chunks of 100,000 lines (what this project does)",
                    duckdb     = "DuckDB, a database engine that scans the file",
                    duckdb_2gb = "DuckDB with its memory capped at 2 GB",
                    whole      = "Whole file in one call (the template)")[method]) |>
  arrange(match(method, c("whole", "chunked", "duckdb", "duckdb_2gb"))) |>
  transmute(Method, `Rows read` = n(rows_read), `Rows kept` = n(rows_kept),
            Seconds = round(seconds), `Peak memory, GB` = formatC(peak_memory_gb, format = "f", digits = 1)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr")

DuckDB is about 26 times faster than either. I kept the chunked import as the project’s method because it is the one the course teaches and it runs only once; DuckDB is what I would reach for if the file had to be read often.

title: Where to eat local in New Orleans
section: What counts as a New Orleans restaurant
text:
What counts as a New Orleans restaurant
A restaurant is any business whose Yelp categories include “Restaurants”, as in the assignment. It is in New Orleans if its coordinates fall inside the official Census boundary of the city. I did not use Yelp’s city field, because it is typed by hand: 57 restaurants labeled “New Orleans” lie outside the boundary, in suburbs such as Elmwood, Jefferson and Harahan, and 4 inside it carry another city name. The boundary gives 2,208 restaurants, 1,355 of them still open when the data end.
Closed restaurants are not ranked, because nobody can go to them. Their reviews are still used to learn each reviewer’s habits.

title: Where to eat local in New Orleans

Figure 3: Most census tracts and block groups hold one or two restaurants.



My choice: two levels. Parts of town answer “which part of the city should I go to”, and Neighborhood Statistical Areas give the detail inside each part.

Census tracts and block groups are too small. The typical one holds one or two restaurants, and four to five of every ten restaurants sit in areas too small to compare.
ZIP code areas and wards are large enough but mean little to a visitor. Nobody plans dinner in “Ward 7” or “70130”, and a single ZIP area holds 32% of the restaurants.
Neighborhoods have names people use, but 40 of the 56 that contain a restaurant have fewer than five, which leaves 22% of restaurants out of any comparison.
Parts of town are how the city is usually described: Uptown, Mid-City, Marigny and Bywater. They are the City Planning Commission’s official grouping of the same neighborhoods, and almost every restaurant sits in a part of town large enough to compare.

The planning district file carries only numbers, so the names are mine, following the names the Commission uses. I labeled District 4 “Mid-City / Tremé / Bayou St. John” instead of the short official “Mid-City”, for a reason that appears in the results.

title: Where to eat local in New Orleans
section: Reviewers, and a score adjusted for their habits
text:
Reviewers, and a score adjusted for their habits
The same four stars mean different things from different people. A reviewer who gives almost everyone five stars is disappointed at four; a reviewer who usually gives three is impressed.
Active reviewers. A reviewer’s habits can only be measured with several reviews. I call a reviewer active with five or more reviews of theme restaurants, the threshold the assignment suggests.


Show code
thresholds |>
  transmute(`Reviews needed` = threshold, `Reviewers kept` = n(reviewers_kept),
            `Share of reviewers` = pct(share_of_reviewers, 1), `Reviews kept` = n(reviews_kept),
            `Share of reviews` = pct(share_of_reviews), `Strict (5th percentile)` = f2(baseline_5th_pct),
            Typical = f2(baseline_median), `Generous (95th percentile)` = f2(baseline_95th_pct)) |>
  kable(align = "rrrrrrrr")

With a threshold of 5, 6,637 reviewers remain. They are only 4.9% of all reviewers but wrote 23% of the reviews. A threshold of 3 keeps more reviews but describes a person from three ratings; a threshold of 10 leaves under a tenth of the reviews.
The baseline is the reviewer’s mean, not the median. Stars are whole numbers, so a median is almost always exactly 4 or 5 (78% of active reviewers) and stops telling reviewers apart.
The adjusted score of a review is its stars minus that reviewer’s mean. The adjusted score of a restaurant is the average of these differences. It is not a new Yelp rating: +0.5 means “active reviewers gave this place half a star more than they usually give”.
Which number ranks the restaurants? I computed both and tested both. The adjusted score is fairer in principle, but it uses under a quarter of the reviews, so it is noisier. On the same 231 restaurants:


Show code
stab_sum |>
  transmute(Ranking = c(ordinary = "Ordinary average, all reviewers", adjusted = "Adjusted score, active reviewers")[ranking],
            `Top-10 members that keep their place, on average` = formatC(average_top10_members_kept, format = "f", digits = 1),
            `Restaurants in the top 10 at least 90% of the time` = restaurants_with_90pct_chance,
            `Restaurants with a realistic chance (5% or more)` = restaurants_with_5pct_chance) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr")

title: Where to eat local in New Orleans
section: How sure is the top ten?
text:
How sure is the top ten?
An average rating is an estimate from the people who happened to write a review. Two tools show how far it can be trusted.
Intervals. For each restaurant, the average plus or minus 1.96 standard errors. Fewer reviews give a wider interval, and overlapping intervals mean two restaurants cannot be ranked with confidence.
Bootstrap. I put each restaurant’s reviews in a hat, drew the same number of reviews back out with replacement, recomputed every average and ranked all 231 restaurants again. Repeating this 2,000 times gives 2,000 versions of the ranking; the chance of being in the top ten is the share of versions in which a restaurant makes it.






Figure 5: The 20 highest averages with their intervals and their chance of being in the top ten.




The exact same ten restaurants come back in 10% of resamples.
On average 8.7 of the ten keep their place.
7 restaurants are in the top ten at least 90% of the time. The last places are contested: Gabrielle Restaurant and Parkway Bakery & Tavern each make the top ten in about half of the resamples.

The honest reading is “7 restaurants that belong in the top ten, and 11 more competing for the last 3 places”.

title: Where to eat local in New Orleans
section: The best part of town
text:
The best part of town
The measure. The question asks where to find the best restaurants, so I score a part of town by the share of its ranked restaurants that are among the city’s best quarter (an average of 4.19 stars or more). It reads as “if I pick a local-food restaurant here, what is the chance it is one of the city’s best?” Only parts of town with five or more ranked restaurants are compared.

The answer is Mid-City / Tremé / Bayou St. John, with 10 great restaurants out of 27 and 3 of the top ten. How strong is that?

It is the most likely leader, not a proven one: first in 50% of resamples and in the first three in 90%. Central City / Garden District is close behind.
It stays first if “great” means the best 20% or the best 33% of the city. With the best 10% only 24 restaurants are left in the whole city, the count per area drops to two or three, and Uptown / Carrollton comes first.
I tried 24 other ways of scoring an area (three sets of restaurants, eight measures). No area wins them all, which is what a close race looks like. The list is in results/area_method_robustness.csv.

The tourist center is not where the best local food is. This part of the answer is firmer. The French Quarter and the CBD together hold 54% of the ranked restaurants, but their average restaurant is rated 3.83 against 4.00 in the rest of the city: a difference of 0.17 stars (95% interval 0.07 to 0.27). On the share of great restaurants the gap points the same way, 21% against 30%, but with this many restaurants it could still be chance (p = 0.16).

title: Where to eat local in New Orleans
section: Limitations
text:
Limitations

The data end in January 2022. “Open” means open then. Some of these restaurants have closed since and new ones are missing.
Yelp reviewers are not a random sample of diners. A rating reflects the people who chose to write, and tourists and residents write for different reasons.
Yelp’s labels are loose. The top ten contains a fried-chicken chain from Tennessee labeled “Southern”. A few steakhouses are in the theme because they carry “Seafood”. The Seafood exception also removes a few places most people would call local, because Yelp gives them a French or Italian label.
155 of the 386 open restaurants are not ranked, because they have fewer than 30 reviews from active reviewers. New and small places are invisible here.
The adjusted score rests on a small group: 4.9% of reviewers, the most active ones. Their taste may differ from an ordinary visitor’s.
Only 7 parts of town could be compared. New Orleans East, Gentilly, Algiers and the Lower Ninth Ward have too few ranked restaurants to say anything.
The bootstrap treats reviews as independent and each reviewer’s usual rating as known. Both are simplifications.
I looked at trial results while choosing the rules. The choice between ranking by the ordinary average or by the adjusted score was made after testing both, on stability, not on which restaurants came out on top. The rules for restaurants were fixed before I looked at parts of town.

Reproduce it
The scripts run in order from the project root. The first one and the benchmark read the raw Yelp files, and scripts 04 and 05 read an intermediate review file that the first one creates. From script 06 on, everything runs from the filtered tables in the repository.

R/02_boundaries.R

R/04_theme_candidates.R
Compares ten candidate themes


R/05_theme.R
Builds the local-food theme, category counts and co-occurrence


R/06_geography.R
Compares the six geographic systems


R/07_scores.R
Reviewer baselines, ordinary average and adjusted score

Top ten, intervals, bootstrap, map

Measures three ways of reading the review file


R/12_site_data.R
Exports the data the story site draws



Package versions are recorded in renv.lock. The random seed is 9426.
